subQuestions.questionText:
There were 11 cars of the same model for sale at a car dealership. The age (in years) of each car and its corresponding selling price (in rands) is provided in the table below.

| Age of car (in years) | Selling price of car (in rand) |
| --- | --- |
| 2 | 293 000 |
| 3 | 265 000 |
| 3 | 256 000 |
| 4 | 219 000 |
| 4 | 241 000 |
| 4 | 246 000 |
| 6 | 226 000 |
| 6 | 176 000 |
| 7 | 154 000 |
| 7 | 180 000 |
| 8 | 148 000 |

Determine the equation of the least squares regression line.
Predict the selling price of a similar car at this car dealership that is 5 years old.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Substitution — $\hat{y} = 331\,397{,}20 - 22\,988{,}32(5)$
Mark 2: Answer — $\hat{y} = 216\,455{,}60$ (or $216\,455{,}61$ by calculator)

subQuestions.questionText: Use the correlation coefficient to show whether the prediction made in QUESTION 1.2 is valid or not.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Strong correlation ($r = -0{,}95$)
Mark 2: The strong correlation suggests the data points lie close to the regression line, therefore the prediction will be valid.

subQuestions.questionText: Use the answer to QUESTION 1.1 to write down the estimated average yearly decrease in the selling price of these 11 cars.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: The average decrease per year is $R22\,988{,}32$.

subQuestions.questionText:
The cumulative frequency table below shows the amount of time that people spent on a particular website on a certain day.

| Time, $t$ (in minutes) | Cumulative frequency |
| --- | --- |
| $0 < t \leq 20$ | 16 |
| $0 < t \leq 40$ | 40 |
| $0 < t \leq 60$ | 59 |
| $0 < t \leq 80$ | 67 |
| $0 < t \leq 100$ | 70 |

How many people visited this website on that day?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: $70$

subQuestions.questionText: How many people spent more than 40 and up to 80 minutes on the website?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: No. of people $= 67 - 40$
Mark 2: $= 27$

subQuestions.questionText: Draw a histogram to represent the information provided in the cumulative frequency table.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks — frequencies per interval: $16 \,;\, 24 \,;\, 19 \,;\, 8 \,;\, 3$):
Mark 1: Two frequencies correct
Mark 2: All frequencies correct
Mark 3: No gaps between the bars

subQuestions.questionText: Comment on the skewness of the data.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: Skewed to the right (positively skewed)

subQuestions.questionText:
There are 9 players in a basketball team. The coach calculated that on average, each player scored 12 points during a game. The points scored by 8 of the 9 players from the team is given below:

| 11 | 14 | 19 | 20 | 8 | 10 | 2 | 14 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

How many players' points score was outside ONE standard deviation of the mean points score?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1: Equating using the mean — $\dfrac{11+14+19+20+8+10+2+14+x}{9} = 12$
Mark 2: The 9th player scored $x = 10$ points
Mark 3: Standard deviation — $\sigma = 5{,}23$ ($5{,}22812$)
Mark 4: Interval — $(\bar{x}-\sigma \,;\, \bar{x}+\sigma) = (12-5{,}23 \,;\, 12+5{,}23) = (6{,}77 \,;\, 17{,}23)$
Mark 5: Answer — 3 players' points were outside one standard deviation of the mean.

subQuestions.questionText:
In the diagram, $P(-1\,;\,8)$, $Q(-4\,;\,-6)$ and $R(12\,;\,2)$ are the vertices of $\triangle PQR$. The angle of inclination of QR is $\theta$.

Calculate the length of QR. Leave your answer in simplified surd form.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: $QR = \sqrt{(-4-12)^2 + (-6-2)^2}$
Mark 2: $= \sqrt{320} = 8\sqrt{5}$ units

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the gradient of QR.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Correct substitution — $m_{QR} = \dfrac{-6-2}{-4-12}$ (or $\dfrac{2-(-6)}{12-(-4)}$)
Mark 2: $m_{QR} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the size of $\theta$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: $\tan\theta = m_{QR} = \dfrac{1}{2}$
Mark 2: $\theta = 26{,}57^\circ$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the equation of QR.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Correct substitution of gradient and point $Q(-4\,;\,-6)$ or $R(12\,;\,2)$ — $-6 = \tfrac{1}{2}(-4) + c$
Mark 2: $y = \tfrac{1}{2}x - 4$

subQuestions.questionText: PQRS, in that order, is a parallelogram. Write down the coordinates of S.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: $x_S = 15$
Mark 2: $y_S = 16$
(Via $Q \to R : (x\,;\,y) \to (x+16\,;\,y+8)$, so $S(15\,;\,16)$.)

subQuestions.questionText: T is a point on QR such that $PT \perp QR$. Calculate the coordinates of T.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1: $m_{PT} = -2$
Mark 2: Equation of PT — $y = -2x + 6$
Mark 3: Equation QR = equation PT — $-2x + 6 = \tfrac{1}{2}x - 4$
Mark 4: Simplification — $-4x + 12 = x - 8 \Rightarrow 5x = 20 \Rightarrow x = 4$
Mark 5: $T(4\,;\,-2)$
(Alternatively: $PQ = \sqrt{205} = PR$, so $\triangle PQR$ is isosceles, the perpendicular height bisects base QR, so T is the midpoint of QR $\Rightarrow T(4\,;\,-2)$.)

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the area of parallelogram PQRS.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: Length of PT — $PT = \sqrt{(4-(-1))^2 + (-2-8)^2} = \sqrt{125} = 5\sqrt{5}$ units
Mark 2: Substitution of QR and PT — Area of PQRS $= QR \cdot PT = (8\sqrt{5})(5\sqrt{5})$
Mark 3: $= 200$ units$^2$

subQuestions.questionText:
In the diagram, $M(p\,;\,q)$ is the centre of the circle that intersects the $x$-axis at A and B. C is a point such that the line drawn from M to C is parallel to the $y$-axis and intersects the $x$-axis at D. MC intersects the circle at $E(-6\,;\,-1)$. Tangents drawn from C touch the circle at A and B. $AD = (q-1)$ units.

Write down the value of $p$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: $p = -6$

subQuestions.questionText: Show that $q = 4$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: $AM = ME = q + 1$ (radii)
Mark 2: $MD = q$
Mark 3: Substitution into Pythagoras — $AM^2 = AD^2 + MD^2 \Rightarrow (q+1)^2 = (q-1)^2 + q^2$
Mark 4: Standard form — $q^2 + 2q + 1 = q^2 - 2q + 1 + q^2 \Rightarrow q^2 - 4q = 0 \Rightarrow q(q-4) = 0$, so $q \neq 0$ or $q = 4$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the equation of the circle in the form $(x-a)^2 + (y-b)^2 = r^2$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: LHS — $AM = 5$ units, $(x+6)^2 + (y-4)^2$
Mark 2: RHS — $= 25$

subQuestions.questionText: If the circle is translated 2 units to the left, determine the minimum distance between the circle and the $y$-axis.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: $3$ units

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the coordinates of A and B.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: Substituting $y = 0$ into the equation of the circle — $(x+6)^2 + (0-4)^2 = 25 \Rightarrow (x+6)^2 = 9$
Mark 2: Coordinates of A — $A(-9\,;\,0)$
Mark 3: Coordinates of B — $B(-3\,;\,0)$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the equation of tangent BC.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: $m_{MB} = \dfrac{4-0}{-6-(-3)} = -\dfrac{4}{3}$
Mark 2: $m_{BC} = \dfrac{3}{4}$
Mark 3: Substitution of gradient BC and coordinates of B — $0 = \tfrac{3}{4}(-3) + c$
Mark 4: Answer — $y = \tfrac{3}{4}x + \tfrac{9}{4}$

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the coordinates of C.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: $x_C = -6$
Mark 2: $y_C = -\dfrac{9}{4}$, so $C\left(-6\,;\,-\dfrac{9}{4}\right)$

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the size of $A\hat{C}B$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: $\tan\alpha = \tfrac{3}{4} \Rightarrow \alpha = 36{,}87^\circ$
Mark 2: $\tan\beta = m_{AC} = -\tfrac{3}{4}$
Mark 3: $\beta = 180^\circ - 36{,}87^\circ = 143{,}13^\circ$
Mark 4: $A\hat{C}B = 106{,}26^\circ$
(Alternatively via the kite/cosine rule: $AC = BC = \tfrac{15}{4}$, $\cos A\hat{C}B = -0{,}28 \Rightarrow A\hat{C}B = 106{,}26^\circ$.)

subQuestions.questionText:
It is given that $\tan 50^\circ = k$. Express EACH of the following in terms of $k$:

$\cos 40^\circ$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks — with $\tan 50^\circ = k$, third side $= \sqrt{k^2+1}$; $\cos 40^\circ = \sin 50^\circ$):
Mark 1: Third side $= \sqrt{k^2+1}$
Mark 2: $\cos 40^\circ = \dfrac{k}{\sqrt{k^2+1}}$

subQuestions.questionText: $\dfrac{2\sin 25^\circ \cdot \cos 25^\circ}{-2 + 4\sin^2 25^\circ}$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1: Numerator $\sin 50^\circ$
Mark 2: Denominator $-2(1 - 2\sin^2 25^\circ)$
Mark 3: Double angle — $= \dfrac{\sin 50^\circ}{-2\cos 50^\circ}$
Mark 4: Substitution OR quotient identity — $= -\tfrac{1}{2}\tan 50^\circ$ (or $\left(\dfrac{k}{\sqrt{k^2+1}}\right) \div \left(\dfrac{-2}{\sqrt{k^2+1}}\right)$)
Mark 5: Answer — $= -\tfrac{1}{2}k$

subQuestions.questionText: $\sin 10^\circ$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: $\sin 10^\circ = \sin(50^\circ - 40^\circ)$
Mark 2: Correct expansion — $= \sin 50^\circ \cos 40^\circ - \cos 50^\circ \sin 40^\circ$
Mark 3: First term — $\left(\dfrac{k}{\sqrt{k^2+1}}\right)\left(\dfrac{k}{\sqrt{k^2+1}}\right)$
Mark 4: Second term — $\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{k^2+1}}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{k^2+1}}\right)$, giving $\dfrac{k^2-1}{k^2+1}$

subQuestions.questionText:
Given: $\dfrac{\sin(540^\circ + x) \cdot \cos(90^\circ + x)}{\sin(-x)}$

Simplify the expression above fully to a single trigonometric ratio.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: $\sin(540^\circ + x) = -\sin x$
Mark 2: $\cos(90^\circ + x) = -\sin x$
Mark 3: $\sin(-x) = -\sin x$
Mark 4: Answer — $\dfrac{(-\sin x)(-\sin x)}{-\sin x} = -\sin x$

subQuestions.questionText: Hence, determine the values of $x$ in the interval $x \in [0^\circ\,;\,360^\circ]$ for which $\sqrt{\dfrac{\sin(540^\circ + x) \cdot \cos(90^\circ + x)}{\sin(-x)}}$ will be real.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Marks 1–2 (double mark): $x \in (180^\circ\,;\,360^\circ)$ (i.e. $180^\circ < x < 360^\circ$)

subQuestions.questionText: Prove that: $\left[\tan(180^\circ - x)\right](1 - \cos^2 x) + \cos^2 x = \dfrac{(\sin x - \cos x)(1 + \sin x \cdot \cos x)}{-\cos x}$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (6 marks — working from the LHS):
Mark 1: $\tan(180^\circ - x) = -\tan x$
Mark 2: $1 - \cos^2 x = \sin^2 x$
Mark 3: Quotient identity — $\left(-\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\right)(\sin^2 x) + \cos^2 x$
Mark 4: Simplification to a single fraction — $\dfrac{\sin^3 x - \cos^3 x}{-\cos x}$
Mark 5: Factors for a difference of cubes — $\dfrac{(\sin x - \cos x)(\sin^2 x + \sin x \cos x + \cos^2 x)}{-\cos x}$
Mark 6: $\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1$, giving $\dfrac{(\sin x - \cos x)(1 + \sin x \cos x)}{-\cos x} = \text{RHS}$

subQuestions.questionText: It is given that $\sin^2 x$; $\cos^2 x$ and $\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x$ are the first three terms of an arithmetic sequence. The constant difference of the arithmetic sequence is NOT zero. Determine the general solution for $x$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (7 marks):
Mark 1: $\cos^2 x - \sin^2 x = \tfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x - \cos^2 x$
Mark 2: $\sin 2x = 2\sin x \cos x$
Mark 3: Standard form — $2\cos^2 x - \sin x \cos x - \sin^2 x = 0$
Mark 4: Factors — $(2\cos x + \sin x)(\cos x - \sin x) = 0$
Mark 5: Both equations — $\tan x = -2$ or $\tan x = 1$ (ref angles $63{,}43^\circ$ and $45^\circ$)
Mark 6: $x = 116{,}57^\circ$ (the $\tan x = 1$ root is rejected: $x \neq 45^\circ + k \cdot 180^\circ$, since the constant difference is not zero)
Mark 7: General solution — $x = 116{,}57^\circ + k \cdot 180^\circ$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$

subQuestions.questionText:
In the diagram, the graph of $f(x) = \cos 2x$ is drawn for $x \in [-135^\circ\,;\,135^\circ]$.

Write down the period of $f$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: $180^\circ$

subQuestions.questionText: On the set of axes provided in the ANSWER BOOK, draw the graph of $g(x) = \tan 2x - 1$ for $x \in [-135^\circ\,;\,135^\circ]$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks — $g$ has asymptotes at $x = -135^\circ, -45^\circ, 45^\circ, 135^\circ$):
Mark 1: Asymptotes
Mark 2: Shape
Mark 3: Intercepts with axes

subQuestions.questionText: Graph $f$ is translated $45^\circ$ to the left to form graph $h$. Determine the equation of $h$ in its simplest form.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: $h(x) = \cos 2(x + 45^\circ) = \cos(2x + 90^\circ) = -\sin 2x$

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the range of $h$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: $y \in [-1\,;\,1]$ (i.e. $-1 \leq y \leq 1$)

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the values of $x$ for which $(1 - \tan 2x)(\cos 2x) \geq 0$ in the interval $x \in [0^\circ\,;\,135^\circ]$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: $\tan 2x = 1 \Rightarrow 2x = 45^\circ \Rightarrow x = 22{,}5^\circ$
Mark 2: $(1 - \tan 2x)(\cos 2x) \geq 0 \Rightarrow (\tan 2x - 1)(\cos 2x) \leq 0$
Mark 3: First interval — $[0^\circ\,;\,22{,}5^\circ]$
Mark 4: Second interval — $[112{,}5^\circ\,;\,135^\circ)$; so $x \in [0^\circ\,;\,22{,}5^\circ] \cup [112{,}5^\circ\,;\,135^\circ)$

subQuestions.questionText:
As part of a school project, learners are required to design a portable stage for a puppet show, as shown in the diagram. The design must fulfil the following requirements:

- BKLC is a horizontal base having $K\hat{B}C = 104^\circ$ and $B\hat{K}C = 52{,}6^\circ$.
- The rectangular backdrop, ABCD, is vertical to the horizontal base and must have an area of $648$ cm$^2$.
- The sides of ABCD must be in the ratio $AB : BC = 1 : 2$.
- The stage must be partly enclosed with triangular sides ABK and DCL.

Show that $AB = 18$ cm.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: $BC = 2AB$, substitution into area of rectangle — Area of ABCD $= BC \times AB \Rightarrow 648 = 2AB \times AB$
Mark 2: $AB^2 = 324 \Rightarrow AB = 18$ cm

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the length of AC.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: $AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 = 18^2 + 36^2$ (Pythagoras)
Mark 2: $AC = \sqrt{1620} = 18\sqrt{5} = 40{,}25$ cm

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the length of diagonal KC.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Substitution into the sine rule — $\dfrac{KC}{\sin K\hat{B}C} = \dfrac{BC}{\sin B\hat{K}C} \Rightarrow \dfrac{KC}{\sin 104^\circ} = \dfrac{36}{\sin 52{,}6^\circ}$
Mark 2: $KC = \dfrac{36\sin 104^\circ}{\sin 52{,}6^\circ} = 43{,}97$ cm

subQuestions.questionText: If $AB = BK$, calculate the size of $K\hat{A}C$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: Length of AK — $AK^2 = AB^2 + BK^2 = 18^2 + 18^2$, so $AK = \sqrt{648} = 18\sqrt{2} = 25{,}46$ cm
Mark 2: Substitution into cosine rule — $KC^2 = AK^2 + AC^2 - 2 \cdot AK \cdot AC \cos K\hat{A}C$, i.e. $(43{,}97)^2 = (18\sqrt{2})^2 + (18\sqrt{5})^2 - 2(18\sqrt{2})(18\sqrt{5})\cos K\hat{A}C$
Mark 3: Simplification — $\cos K\hat{A}C = 0{,}16\ldots$
Mark 4: $K\hat{A}C = 80{,}60^\circ$

subQuestions.questionText:
Provide reasons for your statements in QUESTIONS 9, 10 and 11.

In the diagram, O is the centre of the circle. K, T and P lie on the circle. Use the diagram to prove the theorem which states that the angle subtended by a chord (or arc) at the centre of the circle is equal to twice the angle subtended by the same chord (or arc) at the circumference, that is prove that $T\hat{O}P = 2\,T\hat{K}P$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1: Construction — draw KO produced (to a point, call it the far point on the diameter)
Mark 2: $\hat{O}_1 = \hat{K}_1 + \hat{T}$ (ext $\angle$ of $\triangle$); but $\hat{K}_1 = \hat{T}$ ($\angle$s opp equal sides / radii)
Mark 3: $\therefore \hat{O}_1 = 2\hat{K}_1$
Mark 4: $\hat{O}_2 = \hat{K}_2 + \hat{P}$ (ext $\angle$ of $\triangle$); but $\hat{K}_2 = \hat{P}$ ($\angle$s opp equal sides), so $\hat{O}_2 = 2\hat{K}_2$
Mark 5: $\therefore \hat{O}_1 + \hat{O}_2 = 2\hat{K}_1 + 2\hat{K}_2 = 2(\hat{K}_1 + \hat{K}_2)$, i.e. $T\hat{O}P = 2\,T\hat{K}P$

subQuestions.questionText:
In the diagram, O is the centre of the circle. POF is the diameter of the circle and MF is a tangent to the circle at F. OM cuts the circle at L. $\hat{P} = 32^\circ$.

Calculate, with reasons, the size of $\hat{O}_2$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1 (S): $\hat{O}_2 = 64^\circ$
Mark 2 (R): $\angle$ at centre $= 2 \times \angle$ at circumference (alternatively $P\hat{L}O = \hat{P} = 32^\circ$, $\angle$s opp equal radii; then $\hat{O}_2 = 64^\circ$, ext $\angle$ of $\triangle$)

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate, with reasons, the size of $\hat{M}$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S): $P\hat{F}M = 90^\circ$
Mark 2 (R): tangent $\perp$ diameter
Mark 3 (S): $\hat{M} = 26^\circ$ (sum of $\angle$s of $\triangle$)

subQuestions.questionText:
In the diagram, PQRS is a cyclic quadrilateral. T is a point on the circle such that QT is perpendicular to SR at V. PT and ST are drawn. $\hat{Q}_2 = 35^\circ$ and $\hat{R} = \hat{S}_1$.

Calculate, with reasons, the size of $Q\hat{T}S$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S): $\hat{R} = 55^\circ$ (sum of $\angle$s in $\triangle$)
Mark 2 (S): $Q\hat{T}S = 55^\circ$
Mark 3 (R): $\angle$s in the same segment
(Alternatively: $\hat{S}_2 = 35^\circ$, $\angle$s in the same segment; then $Q\hat{T}S = 55^\circ$, sum of $\angle$s in $\triangle$.)

subQuestions.questionText: Prove that $PQ \parallel SR$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S): $S\hat{P}Q = 125^\circ$
Mark 2 (R): opp $\angle$s of cyclic quad
Mark 3 (R): $\hat{S}_1 = \hat{R} = 55^\circ$ (given); $S\hat{P}Q + \hat{S}_1 = 180^\circ$, so $PQ \parallel SR$ (co-int $\angle$s supp)

subQuestions.questionText: Prove that PT is a diameter of the circle.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1 (S): $\hat{Q}_1 = 90^\circ$ (co-int $\angle$s; $PQ \parallel SR$)
Mark 2 (R): $\therefore PT$ is a diameter (converse $\angle$ in semi-circle / chord subtends $90^\circ$)
(Alternatively: $\hat{S}_2 = 35^\circ$ (ext $\angle$ of $\triangle SVT$), $P\hat{S}T = 90^\circ$, so PT is a diameter.)

subQuestions.questionText:
In the diagram, $\triangle ABC$ is drawn. BA is produced to E. F and D are points on BC such that $AD \parallel EF$. AC and EF intersect at G. $\dfrac{CF}{FB} = \dfrac{2}{5}$ and $\dfrac{CG}{GA} = \dfrac{3}{2}$.

Calculate, with reasons, the value of $\dfrac{FD}{CF}$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1 (S): $\dfrac{FD}{CF} = \dfrac{GA}{CG}$ (prop theorem; $AD \parallel EF$)
Mark 2: Answer — $\dfrac{FD}{CF} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate, with reasons, the value of $\dfrac{BA}{EA}$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks — let $CF = 2x$ so $FB = 5x$):
Mark 1: $FD = \tfrac{2}{3}CF = \tfrac{2}{3}(2x) = \tfrac{4}{3}x$
Mark 2 (S): $\dfrac{BA}{EA} = \dfrac{BD}{FD}$ (prop theorem; $AD \parallel EF$)
Mark 3: Substitution — $\dfrac{BA}{EA} = \dfrac{5x - \tfrac{4}{3}x}{\tfrac{4}{3}x} = \dfrac{11}{3} \times \dfrac{3}{4}$
Mark 4: Answer — $= \dfrac{11}{4}$

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate, with reasons, the value of $\dfrac{\text{Area of } \triangle GCF}{\text{Area of } GFDA}$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks — using $CG:GA = 3:2$ i.e. $CG = 3k, CA = 5k$ and $CF = 3p, CD = 5p$):
Mark 1: $\text{Area } GFDA = \triangle CDA - \triangle CGF$
Mark 2: Numerator — $\text{Area } \triangle GCF = \tfrac{1}{2}(GC)(FC)\sin\hat{C}$
Mark 3: Denominator — $\tfrac{1}{2}AC \cdot CD\sin\hat{C} - \tfrac{1}{2}GC \cdot CF\sin\hat{C}$; so $\dfrac{\tfrac{1}{2}(3k)(3p)\sin\hat{C}}{\tfrac{1}{2}\sin\hat{C}(25kp - 9kp)} = \dfrac{\tfrac{1}{2}(9kp)}{\tfrac{1}{2}(16kp)}$
Mark 4: Answer — $= \dfrac{9}{16}$

subQuestions.questionText:
In the diagram, WVZR is a cyclic quadrilateral. RZ is produced to Q. A tangent is drawn from Q to touch the circle at S. WV is produced to E, a point on ZQ. RW produced meets ZV produced in P. $PQ \parallel WE$. RS and ZS are drawn.

Prove, with reasons, that $PR = \dfrac{PW \cdot QR}{QE}$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1 (S): $\dfrac{QE}{QR} = \dfrac{PW}{PR}$ (prop theorem; $PQ \parallel WE$)
Mark 2 (R): $\therefore PR = \dfrac{PW \cdot QR}{QE}$

subQuestions.questionText: If $\triangle PQZ \;|||\; \triangle RQP$, then $PQ^2 = RQ \cdot QZ$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: $\dfrac{PQ}{RQ} = \dfrac{QZ}{QP}$ ($\triangle PQZ \;|||\; \triangle RQP$), so $\therefore PQ^2 = RQ \cdot QZ$

subQuestions.questionText: $\triangle QSZ \;|||\; \triangle QRS$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks — in $\triangle QSZ$ and $\triangle QRS$):
Mark 1 (S): $\hat{Q}_2 = \hat{Q}_2$ (common $\angle$)
Mark 2 (S/R): $\hat{S}_1 = \hat{R}_2$ (tan chord theorem)
Mark 3 (S or R): $\hat{Z}_1 = Q\hat{S}R$ (3rd $\angle$ of $\triangle$), $\therefore \triangle QSZ \;|||\; \triangle QRS$ ($\angle\angle\angle$)

subQuestions.questionText: $PQ = QS$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S/R): $\dfrac{QS}{QR} = \dfrac{QZ}{QS}$ ($\triangle QSZ \;|||\; \triangle QRS$)
Mark 2 (S): $\therefore QS^2 = QZ \cdot QR$
Mark 3 (S): But $PQ^2 = RQ \cdot QZ$ (proved in 11.2.2), $\therefore PQ = QS$

subQuestions.questionText: $PW = \dfrac{QE \cdot PZ}{\sqrt{QR \cdot QZ}}$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: $\dfrac{PQ}{RQ} = \dfrac{PZ}{PR}$ ($\triangle PQZ \;|||\; \triangle RQP$), so $PR = \dfrac{QR \cdot PZ}{PQ}$
Mark 2 (S): $PR = \dfrac{PW \cdot QR}{QE}$ (proved in 11.2.1), so $\dfrac{PW \cdot QR}{QE} = \dfrac{QR \cdot PZ}{PQ}$
Mark 3: $PW = \dfrac{QE \cdot PZ}{PQ}$
Mark 4: But $PQ^2 = RQ \cdot QZ$ (proved in 11.2.2), so $PQ = \sqrt{RQ \cdot QZ}$, giving $\therefore PW = \dfrac{QE \cdot PZ}{\sqrt{QR \cdot QZ}}$
